unit.title: The well-ordered soul: happiness and harmony
unit.needIt: This helps you understand why it feels hard to stay focused on your goals. It shows how to balance your urges with your long-term plans to find true happiness.
unit.why: A student wants to stop using the internet in class but finds it hard to resist. They learn that making a promise is not enough; they need external rules and a balanced soul to succeed.
unit.outcome: Identify how to balance your inner desires with reason to achieve a well-ordered life.

quiz.q: What did 43% of students do to help themselves stay focused?
quiz.why: The lecture explains that writing down a commitment is a form of pre-commitment.
quiz.quote: 43% of you, 43% of the students in this room made a pre-commitment in the form of a promise.

quiz.why: It is an external constraint that physically prevents the person from using the phone.
quiz.quote: the idea is that you take your cell phone and you put it in this little Ziploc bag, and while you're driving, you are unable to gain access to it.

quiz.q: According to Plato, what is the 'appetitive' part of the soul?
quiz.why: Plato describes the appetitive part as the part full of desires and needs.
quiz.quote: and that we have in addition an appetitive part, which is the which he represents sometimes as a wild horse and sometimes as the multi-headed beast.

quiz.q: How does Plato define a 'just' person?
quiz.why: Plato argues that justice is the health of the soul.
quiz.quote: Roughly, justice is to the soul as health is to the body.

quiz.q: Why does Plato believe that a well-ordered soul leads to happiness?
choices: It allows for a greater form of pleasure.
quiz.why: Plato argues that those who regulate their souls experience a higher form of pleasure than those who only follow their appetites.
quiz.quote: And those of us who have had the great pleasure of doing the second, says Plato, have recognized that that pleasure is a greater form of pleasure than the pleasure of Angry Birds.

quiz.q: What does Jonathan Haidt say about how we experience pleasure?
choices: We only feel pleasure when we reach a goal.
More of something always makes us happier.
Pleasure is only found in material goods.
We are more sensitive to changes than absolute levels.
quiz.why: Haidt explains that humans are sensitive to contrasts, which leads to the hedonic treadmill where we always want more.
quiz.quote: And the second, which hearkens back to the material that we read last week from Daniel Kahneman and the day before that from Jonathan Evans, that because we are more sensitive to changes in goods than to absolute levels of goods, more of something doesn't always make us happier.

quiz.q: What is the 'summum bonum' in Aristotle's work?
quiz.why: Aristotle describes it as the thing pursued for its own sake.
quiz.quote: Sometimes called the highest good, that which is pursued for its own sake.

line.label: A well-ordered soul balances all its parts.

partials: Promises alone are often not enough to change behavior.
External constraints help us stay on track.
The soul has parts that can pull in different directions.
Reason should lead the other parts of the soul.
Happiness comes from a well-ordered and harmonious soul.
crystal.key: True happiness comes from using reason to harmonize our inner desires and actions.

decoys.text: Happiness is just about getting what you want.
decoys.why: Plato and Aristotle argue that unregulated desires lead to a disordered soul, not true flourishing.

decoys.text: Justice is only about following the laws of society.
decoys.why: Socrates argues that justice is an intrinsic health of the soul, not just a set of external rules.

crystal.aha: By using reason to organize our inner parts, we achieve a state of harmony that provides the highest form of happiness.
